questions.prompt: A 4 kg cart moves at 3 m/s. What is its momentum?
questions.misconception: Adding (7), dividing (1.3), or scrambling the numbers (34) comes from skipping the multiplication — momentum is mass × velocity.

questions.prompt: Why is momentum considered a vector quantity?
options: Because it points in the direction of the motion
Because it only has a size
Because it is always a rounded number
Because it is measured in seconds
questions.explanation: Momentum inherits direction from velocity, so it points the way the object moves — like every vector.
questions.misconception: Reading momentum as a plain amount like distance hides its most useful trait: sign and direction matter for conservation.

questions.prompt: Two carts collide. What stays the same before and after the collision?
options: The total momentum of the two carts
The total mass plus a mystery piece
questions.explanation: Momentum is conserved in collisions — the total before equals the total after, even though the carts swap it between them.
questions.misconception: Each cart's own momentum DOES change — but the total naturally holds; that's the conservation core.

questions.prompt: What actually changes an object's momentum?
options: A force acting for a time (impulse = F × Δt)
Moving in a direction without any contact
questions.explanation: A force applied over time — its impulse, F × Δt — is what changes momentum, whether the object speeds up, slows, or turns.
questions.misconception: 'Momentum changes by itself' is a sneaky wrong answer; impulse is the mover, and it is how the conservation balance gets shifted.

questions.prompt: Two objects move at the same speed. Which has more momentum?
options: The one with a brighter color
questions.explanation: Momentum = mass × velocity, so at the same speed the heavier object carries more momentum.
questions.misconception: Same speed doesn't mean same momentum — mass sorts it out, which is why a slow truck hurts more than a fast football.
